en: The *Upāli-dosaka-sūtra*, translated by an unknown person, now appended to the Song Dynasty records.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying in the city of Śrāvastī. He went out from the eastern gate of the city, where there was a woman.
The son’s name was Vūḷhaka; people called her "Mother Vūḷhaka. The Buddha was seated in the upper chamber of Mother Vūḷhaka’s house.

There was a woman who upheld the precepts and observances, named Dūsīkā. On the morning of the fifteenth day of the month, she arose and bathed. She had seven daughters-in-law, all of whom she caused to bathe and dress in fine garments. Before noon, they took their meal; after eating, she washed her hands and led the seven daughters-in-law to where the Buddha was, where they prostrated themselves before him in homage.
The Buddha said,
"Take your seats.
They all withdrew and took their seats.
The Buddha asked Upāli the Śākya:
"Why have you bathed today, put on fine garments, and come to where the Buddha is with your sons and daughters-in-law?
Upāli the Śākya replied:

"Today is the fifteenth day; I have observed the fast. I have heard that there are six days of fasting in a month; I have observed the fast together with my daughter-in-law, not daring to be negligent or lax."
The Buddha told Droṇaśaka:

"The Buddha’s Right Dharma of the Fast consists of eight precepts, which enable people to attain the path that transcends the world, so that they no longer fall into the three evil realms. Wherever they are born, they shall always possess blessings and protection; furthermore, by means of the fundamental causes and conditions of these eight precepts, one attains Buddhahood."
“What is the Buddha’s method of the Right Fasting (upavāsa)?

Here, there is a virtuous person who observes the precepts and fasts on six days of the month: one fast on the eighth day, one fast on the fourteenth day, one fast on the fifteenth day, one fast on the twenty-third day, one fast on the twenty-ninth day, and one fast on the thirtieth day.”
On the day of the fast, rising at dawn, he addressed his household, saying:

"Today my body observes the fast; for this one day, let there be no drinking of alcohol in the house, no quarreling, and no speaking of wealth. Whatever the mind contemplates and whatever the mouth speaks within the household should be in accordance with that of an Arhat."

An Arhat has no intent to kill; on the day of the fast, one who upholds the precepts should likewise be like an Arhat—without intent to kill and without intent to strike. One should be mindful of animals, insects, and moths, wishing them to always live, with a mind such as that of an Arhat; this constitutes the first precept.
"Today and throughout the night, maintain a mind of restraint so as not to kill; to maintain one's intention in this way constitutes one precept of the Buddha.
The Buddha said:

"On the day of the fast, you should maintain your intention like that of an Arhat—free from a greedy mind, having no longing or attachment toward the world, and not even harboring a thought of greed for a blade of grass or a stalk of vegetable."

On days of fasting, one should maintain the mind in this way, as an Arhat does. Those who are wealthy should reflect upon practicing generosity; those who are poor and have nothing should always reflect upon giving. These constitute the two precepts.
The Buddha said:
"On the day of the fast, you should maintain your mind as an arhat does. An arhat does not keep a wife nor does he think of a wife; he does not covet women, nor does he harbor lustful intentions."
"On the day of fasting, one should maintain the mind in this way, as an Arhat; these are the three precepts.
The Buddha said:

"On the day of fasting, one should maintain the mind as an Arhat: do not speak falsely, do not harm the minds of others, and when speaking, speak only the Buddhist scriptures; when not speaking, simply contemplate all that is wholesome."
"On a day of fasting, one should maintain the mind in this way, as an Arhat; these are the four precepts.

The Buddha said, "On a day of fasting, one should maintain the mind as an Arhat does. An Arhat does not drink alcohol; he does not think of alcohol, nor does he contemplate alcohol, for he regards alcohol as evil."
"On the day of fasting, one should maintain the mind in this way, as an Arhat does; this constitutes the five precepts.
The Buddha said:

"On the day of fasting, one should maintain the mind like an Arhat. The mind of an Arhat does not dwell on song and dance; even upon hearing it, he does not take pleasure in the sound of music, nor does his mind dwell on the fragrance of incense and flowers."
"On the day of the fast, one should maintain the mind in this way, as an arhat does; this constitutes the sixth precept.
The Buddha said:
"On the day of the fast, one should maintain the mind like an arhat. An arhat does not lie upon a high or luxurious bed, nor does he even think of lying upon a high or luxurious bed."
"On the day of the fast, one should maintain the mind in this way, as an Arhat does; this constitutes the seventh precept.
The Buddha said:
"On the day of the fast, one should maintain the mind as an Arhat does. An Arhat eats only at midday; after midday until dawn, he must not eat again, though he may drink honey-water."
"On a day of fasting, one who maintains the mind in this manner like an arhat—this constitutes the Eight Precepts.
The Buddha further addressed Upāli the Śākyan:
"Suppose there is a person here whose hair is soiled with grime; he washes his head, and having washed it, he says with joy:"
"I have now removed the grime from my head.
Suppose there is someone who observes the eight precepts for one day and one night; on the following day, they feel joy, and being joyful, they think:
"The precepts of the Buddha's sutras are indeed like this."
"If there is a person whose mind contains evil intentions, these depart immediately; if it contains good intentions, these remain.
The Buddha said, "It is like a person whose body is covered in filth who enters the water to cleanse themselves; all the filth from the body is removed."
Upon emerging from the water, he immediately says with joy:
"My impurities have been removed and my body is light.
Likewise, there are those who observe the fast for one day and one night; on the following day, they immediately rejoice in recollecting the Buddha’s true words, thinking to themselves:
"When shall I attain the Way, so that my mind no longer stirs and no longer runs, and my mind becomes unified, setting its will upon the Way of Non-action?
The Buddha said: "Suppose there is a person whose clothes are covered in much grime; when they obtain ash to wash them and the grime is removed, that person immediately rejoices."
If there is someone who observes the fast for one day and one night, and on the following day feels joy and then thinks of the community of bhikṣus, saying:
"Within the community of bhikṣus, there are those who have attained the stage of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, and arhat."
"Thus one should reflect upon the Saṃgha of bhikṣus.
The Buddha said:
"It is like a person who has a mirror; if the mirror has impurities, once those impurities are polished away, the mirror becomes bright."

If there is a person who observes the fast for one day and one night, possessing a heart of compassion toward all under heaven, and whose mind is opened, clear as light and like a mirror, they should not harbor any thoughts of anger.

If there is someone who observes the fast and precepts for one day and one night, surveys the suffering of the world with compassion, purifies their mind, and rectifies their intentions, reflecting upon the impurities within their own body in this way, they should no longer give way to anger.
The Buddha told Upāli the Śākya:
"One who observes the eightfold fast for one day and one night without fail is superior to one who gives gold, silver, pearls, and gems as offerings to the community of bhikṣus."

In the world there are sixteen great nations: the first is named Aṅga; the second is named Magadha; the third is named Kāśī; the fourth is named Kośala; the fifth is named Vṛji; the sixth is named Pañcāla; the seventh is named Avanti.

The eighth is named Arhatīyu; the ninth is named Jitīyu; the tenth is named Vajrīyu; the eleventh is named Suma; the twelfth is named Sulāṭha; the thirteenth is named Vyatsa; the fourteenth is named Malla; the fifteenth is named Yūni; and the sixteenth is named Kāñcanadī.
Giving precious treasures from these sixteen great kingdoms to the community of bhikṣus is not equal to observing the fast for one day and one night.
Observing the fast enables a person to attain the path that transcends the world; giving away wealth and treasures cannot cause a person to attain the Way.
"Now that I have attained the Buddha-way, it originally arose from these eight precepts.
The Buddha told Droṇaśaka:
"The people of the world are mostly anxious about their household affairs; for this reason, I have established the six monthly fasts and the observance of the eight precepts."

If there are virtuous and good people who wish to quickly attain the path of an Arhat, or who wish to swiftly attain the path of a Buddha, or who wish to be reborn in the heavens, and who are able to rectify their own minds and unify their intentions, it is well for them to observe the fast on fifteen days of the month, and it is also well to observe the fast on twenty days of the month.
Because people have many anxieties regarding household affairs, [the Buddha] has provided the six fast days of the month.

Regarding the six-day fast: it is like the water of the great ocean, which cannot be measured by pecks; likewise, for one who observes the fast and precepts for even a single day and night, their merit is incalculable.
The Buddha told Upāli the Śākya:
"First take your son and daughter-in-law back home, and then recite and keep these eight precepts of the Right Fasting (Upoṣadha).
Having received this instruction, Upāli the Śākya prostrated before the Buddha and departed.
The Sūtra on Upavīra Falling from the Śākya Clan.
